149	
150	- `research/extracts/`: the POPL 2019 paper, Steele's talks of 2015 and 2016, and the project's web sites with the post of July 2012 that ended the project;
151	- the reading of the team's 2012 patents: `explorations/reviews/mie-probes/patents-forest-rule.md`.
152	
153	If a conflict or a decision not taken needs the designers' reason for a rule, print the row of its design area. WORD is a word of the area, such as `coercion`, `juxtaposition`, `dispatch` or `Arrays`. A word can match several rows, each about 1 to 2 KB.
154	
155	    explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:design-intent-sources.md#The map, by design area@WORD'
156	
157	Then open the sources that the row names. Among them are the `\note{}` boxes and the team's written rationale in the Internal Document appendix: `Specification/appendices/FAQ.tex` and `future.tex`. The row also names the later works that speak to its area, after the words "after the repository (§7)". To read what one of them covers and does not cover, print its row of the map's section "After the repository". WORD is a word of its title, such as `Polymorphic`, `patents`, `JuliaCon` or `Wrapping`. A row is about 1 to 2 KB.
158	
159	    explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:design-intent-sources.md#After the repository@WORD'
160	
161	When your report describes the team's sources on a question, say which of them is one of the late positions above. If the question is about a type rule, also name each later work that you checked.
162	
163	## The procedure
164	
165	1. Search the record with the queries in `records.md`. If two of the team's sources disagree, look for the construct in `revival-changes.md` before you search the record.
166	2. If the record or `revival-changes.md` settles the question, go back to building. Cite what settles it.
167	3. If you have evidence against a decision of the curator, read its POSITIONS entry and the notes that it names. If the decision used your evidence, go back to building.
168	4. Search the original tree. These help: the feature table and the phase map (`compiler.md`, "Before an edit"), the `\note{}` boxes and the map of design areas ("Weighing the sources" above), and the history of a file (`records.md`, "The repository's history").
169	5. Before you write that something does not exist, search the record for it, INDEX included (`index:WORDS`).
170	6. Decide whose choice it is, by "The choices that are yours" above.
171	7. Record each defect that you found as `tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded", says. If you make the choice and repair the defect, that is its item 1. If the question stays open, it is its item 3. Record a finding that is not a defect, such as a fact about the original tree, as `records.md`, "Writing to the record", says.
172	8. If your brief does not let you edit the ledger, put the ledger row in your report:
173	   1. Write the row in a file, in the form that `records.md` gives for a new row.
174	   2. Run `python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py check --rows FILE`. It counts the `?` in the number cell as a broken rule. Correct the row until the check names no other rule.
175	   3. Copy the row into your report.
176	9. If the question touches a passage of the specification, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.
177	10. If the choice is yours, make it. Report it as a decision.
178	11. If the choice is the curator's, report it as a decision not taken. Give these:
179	    - the question;
180	    - each source, and its date ("Weighing the sources" above says what else to note);
181	    - each possible solution, and what it changes;
182	    - which solution keeps the current behaviour.
183	12. If you cannot get some evidence in your task, say in your report what is missing and how to get it.
184	# Committing and pushing
185	
186	**scratch**
187	: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.
188	
189	Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.
190	
191	## What to commit
192	
193	- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
194	- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
195	- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
196	- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
197	- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
198	- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
199	- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.
200	
201	## How to commit
202	
203	Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:
204	
205	    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>
206	
207	- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
208	- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
209	- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
210	- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
211	- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
212	- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:
213	
214	      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
215	      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
216	
217	  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.
218	
219	## Pushing
220	
221	Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.
222	
223	- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
224	- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree does not delete its branch, which stays. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
225	- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
226	  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
227	  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
228	  3. If it lists only your commits, push the three refs with this one command, and wait for it to end:
229	
230	         git push --atomic origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable
231	
232	     With `--atomic`, the three refs update together or not at all. Do not pipe the command into another command, since a pipe hides a refusal. A refusal shows as a line that starts with `!`, and as a non-zero exit. The last ref keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
233	- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
234	- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and do not run it again. Report the refused ref and git's message.
235	# Setting up, building, the caches, and what to rebuild
236	
237	**tree**
238	: Checkout of the repository: the main checkout or a worktree. In a command, `<tree>` is the tree that you work in: the one that your brief names, else the one that your session starts in.
239	
240	**library order**
241	: Five compiles that build the compiled path's library into the caches.
242	
243	**DSL grammar**
244	: `grammar` declaration in an api, which adds syntax for a domain-specific language.
245	
246	**parser directory**
247	: New `fortress<random>rats` folder of 5.8 MB, in which a program that imports a DSL grammar gets a Rats! parser generated when it runs. The run makes it in its JVM's temporary directory and never deletes it.
248	
249	## Setting up each call
250	
251	Start every Bash call with these lines. They put you at the tree's root, where this skill's commands start unless they `cd`:
252	
253	    cd <tree> && mkdir -p tmp
254	    export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
255	    export FORTRESS_HOME=$PWD FORTRESS_THREADS=1 TMPDIR=$PWD/tmp JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"
256	    unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
257	
258	- If `/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64` or `ant` is missing, run `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y openjdk-25-jdk-headless ant` first.
259	- `bin/fortress` takes `FORTRESS_HOME` from the shell whenever it is set. If it names another tree, you run that tree's code. Check it with `echo $FORTRESS_HOME`.
260	- `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` is unset, because the proxy's trust-store flags in it break ant's JVM forks.
261	
262	The lines give the settings of `explorations/experiment/env.sh`, with two differences:
263	
264	- The JVM's temporary directory is your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
265	- They leave out env.sh's removal of old parser directories in `/tmp`, because your runs put theirs in your tree's `tmp/` (below).
266	
267	If your brief tells you to run `source env.sh` and then to point `TMPDIR` and `JAVA_FLAGS` at `tmp/`, use the lines above. They do the same.
268	
269	The library and microGPT import no DSL grammar, and of the gated tests only `ProjectFortress/syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss` does. The ungated tests beside it import one, and so do the APL experiments under `explorations/apl/`.
270	
271	With the lines above, your runs that import a DSL grammar put their parser directories in `<tree>/tmp/`. Hundreds of them once filled the disk allowance. So:
272	
273	- When no run of yours is live, remove yours: `rm -rf <tree>/tmp/fortress*rats`.
274	- Before a long run, check `df -h /`. How to read it: the `cloud-container` skill.
275	
276	## Two layers of code
277	
278	The repository holds two layers of code. Different tools build them, at different times, so "compile" means a different thing in each layer.
279	
280	The implementation is the parser, walk, the compiled checker, the code generator and the runtime. It is the Java and Scala under `ProjectFortress/src/`, with the parser grammars (`parser/*.rats`) and the syntax tree generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`. `ant compileAll` builds it into `ProjectFortress/build/` ("Building", below). `ant compile` is another name for it.
281	
282	The Fortress code is the library, the tests and the programs: the `.fss` and `.fsi` files. The `fortress` commands run the phases on it and keep the results in the caches:
283	
284	- Walk runs the phases on each component that a run needs. It needs no `fortress compile`.
285	- `fortress compile` writes a component's jar. It is for the compiled path's components only: the compiler's library, compiled tests and compiled programs.
286	- `fortress run` compiles no Fortress source.
287	- A command reuses an entry if no source that the entry depends on is newer than the entry: its own source, and the `.fsi` files of the apis that it imports, at any depth.
288	
289	An edit makes stale what was built from it:
290	
291	- Java or Scala: the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/`. Run `ant compileAll`. The cache entries that the edited code wrote are stale too, and no entry notices it: an entry is compared with its sources, never with the implementation. For example, after a change to a native helper's signature, its old wrapper stays in `nativewrapper_cache/`, and the run links the old signature. For this reason, the build deletes the caches when the implementation changes ("Building").
292	- A parser grammar: the generated parser, and every entry that it parsed. Run `ant compileAll`.
293	- A `.fss` or `.fsi` file of the library: the entries of that component, and after an `.fsi` edit, the entries of every component that imports the api. Walk analyses them again by itself. A component of the compiler's library needs a compile, or the library order ("After an edit of the library").
294	- A test or a program: its own entries. Walk and the harness analyse a walk test again by themselves. Compile a compiled test or program again, or let the harness do it.
295	
296	## The caches
297	
298	All the caches are gitignored. A caches folder also holds:
299	
300	- `environment_cache/`: another cache of walk's.
301	- `nativewrapper_cache/`: the wrappers for the Java classes that an api imports with `import java`.
302	- `global.map`: the linker's saved state, an empty map in practice. If it is missing, the linker writes an empty one, also in a private caches folder.
303	- `implementation.stamp`: the stamp of the build that the caches belong to ("Building", below).
304	
305	Only these runs read `default_repository/caches`: `fortress compile`, `fortress run`, `fortress junit` (and `junit.sh`), `ant testOnly`, and a direct walk run. These runs use private caches (`-Dfortress.caches` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`), and need neither the library order nor warm caches: `harness-one.sh`, the gate's ladder regression (`gate.md`) and both ant suites. `harness-one.sh` keeps its private cache beside its scratch folder between calls (`tests-running.md`).
306	
307	## The library order
308	
309	The first of its compiles, `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, holds the top type `Any`, which both libraries share. The other four are the compiler's own. All five take about 100 to 110 s after `ant compileAll`.
310	
311	Run it only when the caches lack the library's jars, or hold stale ones:
312	
313	- after a build that printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, and in a tree whose caches are empty;
314	- after an edit of a library `.fsi` that the section "After an edit of the library" names.
315	
316	Otherwise the jars are in place, and a compiled test or program needs no library order. The five commands:
317	
318	    cd ProjectFortress
319	    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss            # 17 s
320	    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss    # 63 s
321	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss        # 27 s
322	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss        # 2 s
323	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss         # 2 s
324	
325	Before the first compiled run, check that `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/` holds five jars: `fortress.AnyType.jar`, `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`, `fortress.CompilerLibrary.jar`, `fortress.CompilerAlgebra.jar` and `CompilerSystem.jar`, which has no prefix. Sometimes all five compiles exit 0 and a jar is missing. The cause is not known.
326	
327	- If a jar is missing, run the five commands again. Once, this made the jars.
328	- If a jar is still missing, report it as a defect. Quote the commands, their exit codes and the folder's listing.
329	- Keep the caches in this case too. Once, emptying them made the jars, but a deletion hides the cause.
330	
331	## Name resolution
332	
333	- `fortress.source.path` searches `.` (the current directory) first, then `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin`, `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/test_library`. The first `Foo.fsi` or `Foo.fss` that it finds wins. So a file in the directory that you run from hides the library's file of the same name.
334	- A component's file name without `.fss` must be the component's name.
335	- If both libraries use one api name, one of them breaks. For this reason, the compiler's apis have the `Compiler` prefix.
336	- The top-level `CompilerLibrary/` holds `.fsi`-only stubs, not `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss`. `lib/` holds Fortress sources, not jars.
337	- If paths behave wrongly, read `repository/ProjectProperties.java`. It resolves `FORTRESS_HOME`, `BASEDIR` and the cache paths.
338	
339	## Building
340	
341	Run `ant compileAll` from the tree's root. It is the only build: `ProjectFortress/build.xml` is a stub.
342	
343	- It makes the parser and the syntax tree again only if their sources changed.
344	- javac compiles only the changed Java files and the files that depend on them. scalac runs only if its inputs changed, and then compiles every Scala file.
345	- It decides by a stamp whether it deletes the caches. `ProjectFortress/build/implementation.stamp` is a hash of the built implementation, and each caches folder holds the stamp of the build that filled it. At its end, the build keeps `default_repository/caches` if its stamp equals the new one, and empties it if not. It does not touch a private caches folder. It prints `Caches <folder> kept` or `Caches <folder> started again, empty`. The comment "The caches and the implementation" in `build.xml` gives the rule.
346	- `ant cleanCache` deletes the caches, whatever their stamp.
347	- With nothing changed, it takes about 4 s. After an edit, it takes about 25 to 60 s on an idle machine, scalac about 19 s of it, and about 50 to 80 s on a new or cleaned tree. While other agents build, it takes up to about 140 s.
348	- After a build that started the caches again, yours or a test target's, run the library order before the next compiled run. So each edit of Java or Scala costs about 2 to 3 minutes before a compiled run: the build, then the library order.
349	- If it fails, fix the error and run the same command again. Clear nothing by hand.
350	
351	## After an edit of the library
352	
353	The compiled path sees an edit of its library only when you compile the edited component itself. Compiling your own program never recompiles the library under it.
354	
355	- If you edited the `.fss` of one of the five library components, and not its `.fsi`: run `fortress compile` on that component only. Programs need no recompile.
356	- If you edited the `.fsi` of AnyType, CompilerBuiltin, CompilerLibrary or CompilerAlgebra: run the whole library order. Every api depends on these four.
357	- If you edited `CompilerSystem.fsi`: compile CompilerSystem only.
358	- If you edited any other file of `Library/` or `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: it is walk's library. Do nothing: walk reads it again, and compiled programs do not link it yet.
359	
360	## Symptoms of a skipped step
361	
362	If you skip the step for your edit, the run shows it:
363	
364	- After an edit of a body, the run uses the old code and gives no warning.
365	- After an edit of an api, the run stops with `NoSuchMethodError` or `NoClassDefFoundError` on a library member. Examples: `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.println`, `coerce_ZZ32`, `fortress/CompilerLibrary$GeneratorZZ32`. The run found no library jar and used the bootstrap stubs: old class files of the compiler's library that the build compiles from `ProjectFortress/src/fortress/` into `ProjectFortress/build/fortress/`.
366	
367	If you see either, do the step now: recompile the component, or run the library order. Do not delete the caches to fix it. A deletion works only because it repeats the library order and every analysis from cold. If something else looks like a stale cache, find its cause before you delete anything.
368	
369	Two messages look like a skipped step, but usually show a defect:
370	
371	- A `NoSuchMethodError` on a method of your own program, often with a mangled name such as `\=tag?1??Arrow...`, is a defect of the compiled path. Record it (`tests-writing.md`).
372	- "Unable to read serialized data for X, recommend you delete the Fortress bytecode cache and relink" is usually a defect of the code generator. Search the gap ledger for the message. Run the library order only if X is a member of a `Compiler*` or `AnyType` component. Keep the caches, whatever the message advises.
373	
374	Two more facts help you read a run:
375	
376	- A `fortress compile` of a source that did not change, and whose jar exists, writes nothing and exits 0.
377	- A library compile that failed or was killed wrote nothing, or only its jar. Programs link the old jar with no warning until you fix the error and compile that component again.
378

3	# The switch-over rehearsed by brute force
4	
5	The question: what stands between today's tree (`832f7d0d91`) and a program that compiles to bytecode and runs against the interpreter's library (P-37, P-33)? The method: switch a scratch tree's compiled path onto that library by the smallest change, then push, hacking past each wall, and record the walls in the order met. A hack is marked as one in the patch (`SWITCH HACK`), and the patch is not a design.
6

8	
9	How the runs were made: the edited Java and Scala classes compiled into a scratch folder put first on the class path (the `fortress-repo` skill's `compiler.md`, "Testing an edit here"), with a private caches folder that started empty; one `ant compileAll` after the run-time classes changed.

- P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of unboxed doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** Why: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers. Today the code generator boxes every number: an `RR64` value is an object of the class `FRR64`. In Java models of microGPT's three array kernels, the dot product, the matrix product and the row lift, boxing is the main cost (F-11 holds the measurement). How arrays store doubles, as `double[]`, is P-84's decision.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:41
- P-43 **The exclusion rule stays, and the number tower is flat (route A).** The compiled checker keeps the multiple instantiation exclusion rule. So the library's numbers are flat, as the team (Chase, Ryu, Maessen and Allen) flattened the compiler prelude in 2009 and 2010. The fixed widths, `ZZ`, `QQ` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`, each with its own algebra, and `Number` has no catch-all operators. Why: the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way, and its route leads to the POPL 2019 paper, which keeps the rule. He cares that specialised code runs fast, not how a specialisation is chosen. F-46 prices a return to route C.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Arrays and the model program

POSITIONS.md:110
- P-84 **On the compiled path, the array of every number type is to be stored unboxed, in a Java array of its primitive type, and every array is to have the most efficient store that its element type allows; arrays keep the team's `nat` sizes in their types.** `RR64` goes in a `double[]`, `ZZ32` in an `int[]`, and so on, for each number type that has a Java primitive type; `RR64`'s `double[]`, the model's, is the first case. Why: a high-performance language cannot box its array elements, and the sizes are central to the team's design. So the storage and the sizes are one design: the sizes stay in the array types as `nat` static parameters, as the library's `Vector` and `Matrix` declare them, and the compiled checker checks them. The sizes do not wait while a first version of the store carries them only as run-time fields; that layered plan was rejected. Both halves follow the library's own patterns (P-27, on extending the library in its own way). The compiled checker checks `nat` static parameters (F-67). The class loader, as it makes a generic instance's class, only renames the type parameter, so it gives no instance a `double[]` field; a loader that would, way A4 of array decision A (P-85), is unmeasured (F-18).

POSITIONS.md:111

The three questions: how the array factory chooses the store of each element type; whether the store also keeps the size as a field, beside the size in the type; and whether a factory for a size known only at run time returns the unsized `Array[\E,I\]`, whose type holds no size. These questions are apart from decisions A, B and D: decision A is how an array of a number type, made through the library's generic array traits, gets its unboxed store, `RR64`'s `double[]` first (P-84); B is where unboxed arithmetic happens; and D is the sizes in the model's own types (P-87). Tests: `compiler_tests/ExtendsGenericAtAnyCompiled.test`, `ForbidClauseCompiled.test`, `TestModifierCompiled.test`; for row 890, `XXXFinallyOnEscape.test`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-codegen-walls/REPORT.md`, sections 1, 2 and 5; `reviews/batch-25-review.md`, "Where the text, the brief or the principles split", 3 and 4.
155:- F-328 **Walk answers the compiled helpers `stringOps.typeName` and `equality.sEquiv` with its own operations, and its ilk names the five native number objects by their traits.** The one library binds `Object.ilkName` to `stringOps.typeName` and `SEQV` over `Any` to `equality.sEquiv` (P-58's form); walk's loader maps the two names, before it looks for a helper, to `ObjectPrims$ClassName` and `AnyPrim$SEquiv` (`interpreter/glue/NativeApp.java`, `OWN_OPERATIONS`, a table that holds `runtime`'s six names too, F-335), so it never loads the two helpers. `Object.asString` is `self.ilkName`. Walk's ilk prints `Int`, `Long`, `BigNum`, `Float` and `UnsignedLong` of `FortressBuiltin` as `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `RR64` and `NN64`, also inside static arguments, tuples and arrows; other types, strings, `Char` and `Ratio` among them, keep their names, and walk instantiates a generic at the trait (F-344). Tests: `tests/AnyNativesIntrinsicWalk`, `compiler_tests/AnyNativesIntrinsicCompiled`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-any-carrier/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".
158:- F-333 **The one library's arrays hold their elements in a Java-backed store in a field, which walk answers with its own `AtomicArray`.** `NativeArray` is a plain component: `PrimitiveArray` and `PrimImmutableArray` hold a `JavaArrayStore` of `FortressLibrary` in the field `mem` and read through `cast[\T\]`, `PrimImmutableRR64Array` a `JavaRR64ArrayStore`, now in the api with no factory choosing it (P-84, P-85). The stores' 7 bindings name `nativeHelpers/arrayOps` over the compiled `FortressArrayStore`, an `Object[]` whose elements the compiled transaction keys by array and index (`TXReadSlot`, `TXWriteSlot`), and `FortressRR64ArrayStore`, a `double[]`; NamingCzar's walk-world table reads the two classes as the two traits. Walk's loader answers each `arrayOps` name with `ArrayOps$<name>` over `FortressBuiltin`'s private `JavaArrayStoreObject`, an `AtomicArray`, and `JavaRR64ArrayStoreObject`, a `double[]`, and refuses a name with no operation at load. A second initialisation is ignored in both arrays, by walk's store and by `FortressArrayStore` (row 466); the two RR64 stores write it and answer `true`, as `PrimImmutableRR64Array`'s glue did. The stores' 7 bindings leave glue classes (F-299 holds the count). Tests: `tests/ArrayStoreWalk`, `ArrayStoreRR64Walk`, `ArrayInitOnceWalk`, `ArrayOpsMisspeltWalk`, `compiler/runtimeValues/ArrayStoreJUTest`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-array-store/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".
165:- F-344 **Under walk, a value of the five native number objects or of the four string objects is read at its trait where walk infers a static argument, and walk's type text prints each of the nine by its trait.** `Int`, `Long`, `BigNum`, `Float` and `UnsignedLong` of `FortressBuiltin` read and print as `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `RR64` and `NN64`; `FlatString`, `CatString`, `EmptyString` and `SubString` as `String`; also inside tuple types; each told by its declaring component (`interpreter/evaluator/types/LanguageTypes.java`), at `EvaluatorBase`'s three reads and in `FTraitOrObject.toString`. So `Cell(3)` is a `Cell[\ZZ32\]`, `Cell("s")` a `Cell[\String\]`, `<|1, 2, 3|>` an `ArrayList[\ZZ32\]`, and messages and `Reflect` print `ZZ32` where they printed `Int`; a float numeral, an `RR64` value (F-341), reads at `RR64`. The types keep their names: a `typecase` arm `Int` still matches `3`, and the ilk still names a string object by its own name, `FlatString`. Test: `tests/LanguageTypeInstancesWalk`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-language-types/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".
197:- F-123 **A compiled object with no `asString` of its own prints its bare type name, as walk does.** A value whose run-time Java class declares its own `toString`, such as the compiled `RR32`'s, prints by it. Open on the compiled path: through the prelude's `Object`, an object that declares or inherits a zero-argument Fortress member named `toString` overflows the stack when it is printed (row 321), though not through the one library's `Object`, whose `asString` is `self.ilkName`; and `asDebugString` and `asExprString` print differently from walk's, where the specification is silent (row 363). For a string static argument both paths give `Cell[\String\]`, the specification's answer, walk reading a string object at `String` (F-344). For a numeral argument both paths give the numeral's default, the specification's answer: `Cell(3)` is a `Cell[\ZZ32\]` (`tests/LanguageTypeInstancesWalk`, `compiler_tests/LiteralDefaultCompiled`; F-341, F-342). Gated by `compiler_tests/DefaultRenderRungS`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-default-rendering/REPORT.md`, "Defects and their homes".
204:- F-131 **The one library's number tower is flat.** It builds P-43. `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR64`, `RR32` and the numerals' trait `Numeral` are siblings under `Number`; below `Numeral` lie the numeral types `NaturalNumeral` and `RadixPointNumeral`, which each of the eight converts from (F-79). The compiled checker gives a numeral its numeral type and converts it where it stands (F-342); walk gives it its default, `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit, and converts it where its place fixes a type (F-341). Each wider integer type converts from each narrower one, and `RR64` from a `ZZ32`; a `ZZ64` goes into `RR64` only when written out (P-74). `QQ` converts from the five integer types, and `RR64` converts from `RR32` too (F-139). `NN32` does not yet convert into `RR64`: P-75 decides that it will. `Number` declares no `=`; each number type declares one at each number type it coerces from or into (F-324). Under walk `SUM <|1, 2, 3|>`, with no static argument, is 6, its list read at `ZZ32` (F-344), and an empty `SUM` over an additive group that is not a number dies (row 436). Gated by `tests/FlatTowerRungF.fss` for every type but `RR32` and the numeral types: that none is another's subtype, their coercions and `=`. `RR32`'s place is gated with F-139, and the numeral types' with F-79. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-flat-tower/REPORT.md` sections 5 and 17.

# Who wrote Fortress — an authorship map

Compiled 2026-08-21 from the git history (5,397 historical commits,
2007-01-04 → 2012-08-31) plus the 1.0 specification's acknowledgments,
the project's published papers, and public-web checks. Purpose: know who
wrote which subsystem, and whom one could plausibly contact with
questions about history or unrealized plans.

**Caveats.** The git record starts January 2007; the project began in 2003,
so four years of design history (and any pre-2007 code) predate every count
below — Eric Allen, for instance, was co-principal-investigator from the
start but shows only ~233 commits because the record starts late, and spec
co-authors **Sam Tobin-Hochstadt** and **Joe Hallett** have *zero* commits
here (their era's record is lost). Counts are `git log --full-history`
per path. Plain `git log -- <dir>` — and `git blame` — are broken in this
repository: the hg→git conversion behind the GitHub mirror
`sirinath/fortress`, of which this repository is a 2018 fork (see
`explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`), severed 146 parent links, turning
ordinary 2011–2012 java.net-era commits
into parentless full-tree snapshots, so any history walk from HEAD dead-ends
at the nearest phantom root instead of reaching 2007 (blame will credit an
entire untouched file to, e.g., a July 2012 seam commit). Those snapshot
roots also add up to ~146 spurious per-path "touched" credits inside the
`--full-history` counts — noise spread across 2011–12 committers, small at
the scale of the numbers above. In the other direction, the counts
*undercount* the 2008 research-branch authors: those branches were
svn-squash-merged into trunk, so the fine-grained per-commit record for
Culpepper, Rafkind, Lee, and Spiegel on that work survives only on the
relic branch heads, not in any walk from HEAD — see "The relic branches"
below. The
2007–2011 SVN/Mercurial history uses bare usernames (`sukyoungryu@localhost`
etc.); identities are resolved below with the evidence stated.

## The identity key

Three naming eras: Sun employee IDs (Jan–Jun 2007), SVN usernames
(June 2007 on), and real names (after the March 2011 move to Mercurial on
java.net). The ID→username handoffs are datable to days — each ID stops
committing within a week of its username starting, on the same files.

| **David Chase** (991) | dc12360, dr2chase, David Chase | 2007-01 → 2012-07 | Certain — spec co-author; `dr2chase` is his GitHub handle; owned the 2011 java.net migration |

| **Christine H. Flood** (261) | chf, chmf | 2007-01 → 2012-05 | **Verified**: her own bio — PLRG work on "the bytecode optimizer, software transactional memory, and compilation to a fork/join framework" — matches her commits exactly |
| **Justin Hilburn** (261) | jrhil47 | 2008-05 → 2011-09 | High — OOPSLA 2011 co-author; commits are overloading/OverloadingOracle, the paper's subject |
| **Jon Rafkind** (237) | jon | 2008-05 → 2009-08 | High — all `[syntax]` commits; *Growing a Syntax* (FOOL 2009) co-author |
| **Eric Allen** (233) | ea144895, EricAllen | 2007-06 → 2011-07 | Certain — spec co-author, co-PI with Steele |
| **Guy L. Steele Jr.** (177) | gls, Guy Steele | 2008-07 → 2012-06 | Certain |

[compiler] Usability improvements:
After last checkin, that caused us to report compilation errors when
running link, also made sure compilation set the error code so that
shell commands would realize the failure had happened.
Error messages were previously reformatted to put source locations on
a single line, but to make editors happy source locations ought to be
colon-separated when they initiate a location message in this way.
That required fixing the reporting code (easy) and fixing the matching
in the tests (tedious, and the reason why this diff is so long).
Finally, some whitespace fixups because some stuff was edited by a
four-space-using-tabs editor.  Please switch off tabs!  If you use
emacs I have some code kicking around.

content.content:
## Natives

The library binds each of walk's natives by a declaration whose body is `builtinPrimitive("…")`. The string names one of these:

- A glue class, as `com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.X`, in `interpreter/glue/prim/`. A glue class takes walk's `FValue` objects, so the compiled path cannot use it.
- A helper: a public static method of a class under `nativeHelpers/`, as `com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.<method>`. `interpreter/glue/StaticNativeApp.java` calls it by reflection, with a method's `self` first. The compiled path calls it too (`compiler.md`, "Natives"). Most bindings name a helper. The others name a glue class. F-299 counts both kinds (`records.md`, "Reading the record").

Walk carries each declared type of a helper's binding in one Java type:

- `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `Char` in `int`; `ZZ64` and `NN64` in `long`; `RR64` and `Float`, the library's object that extends `RR64`, in `double`; `RR32` in `float`; `Boolean` in `boolean`;
- `FlatString` and `JavaString` in `String`, and `String` too, except as a parameter other than `self`; `ZZ` in `BigInteger`; `()` in `void`; `JavaBufferedWriter` and `JavaBufferedReader`, the library's writer and reader traits, in `compiler/runtimeValues/FortressBufferedWriter` and `FortressBufferedReader`, which the checker reads back as the two traits.

In a method, walk carries `self` by the type that declares the method:

Each of \KWD{extends}, \KWD{excludes}, and \KWD{comprises} clauses consists
of \KWD{extends}, \KWD{excludes}, and \KWD{comprises}
respectively followed by a set of trait references
separated by commas and enclosed in braces `\txt{\{}' and `\txt{\}}'.
If such a clause contains only one trait, the enclosing braces may be elided.
In an API (but not a component),
a \KWD{comprises} clause may include ``\EXP{\ldots}''.
A trait reference listed in the \KWD{comprises} clause is a declared
trait identifier (within the same component or an API imported by the
component).
\note{
listed type, as in the clause of the trait \TYP{NatParam} of \library,
which the team wrote as a comment and the revival restores.}
\note{
If the \KWD{comprises} clause of a trait \VAR{T} includes ``\EXP{\ldots}''
(and must therefore be in an API),
then in a component exporting the enclosing API,
other traits may explicitly extend \VAR{T},
but these traits may not be declared or imported by the API
(see \secref{apis}).}

A trait declaration of \VAR{T} that has no \KWD{comprises} clause,
or one that lists no type but ``\EXP{\ldots}'', may have a \emph{self-type parameter}:
a static parameter \VAR{X} of \VAR{T}
whose bounds include \VAR{T} at its own static parameters,
as in \EXP{\KWD{trait}\;T\llbracket{}X \KWD{extends} T\llbracket{}X\rrbracket\rrbracket},
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} is no longer a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, which coerces from it.
The library's integer types hold no infinite value.
A generic call over two different integer types infers the
narrowest type that both coerce into, by the rule of
\chapref{type-inference}, and need not write its static argument: with
\VAR{a} of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and \VAR{b} of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64},
\EXP{f(a, b)} infers \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, as \EXP{f\llbracket\mathbb{Z}64\rrbracket(a, b)} writes it.}

content.content:
\section{Value Objects}
\seclabel{value-objects}

An object declaration with the modifier \KWD{value} declares a value object
that is called in many languages a \emph{primitive} value.
The \objecttype\ declared by a value object implicitly has the modifier
\KWD{value}.



The fields of a \KWD{value} object are immutable;
they cannot be changed directly or it is a static error.
However, Fortress allows value objects to have settable fields
as an abbreviation for constructing a new value object with a different
value for one field.
If a value object has a setter method or a subscripted assignment operator
method (described in \secref{subscripted-assignment}),
then the return type of the method must be the value object trait type
instead of \EXP{()}.  When such a method is invoked, the receiver
must itself be assignable, and the value returned by the method
is assigned to the receiver.


For example, here is a value object \TYP{Complex} number:
%value object Complex(settable real:Double, settable imaginary:Double=0)
%  opr +(self,other:Complex) = Complex(real + other.real, imaginary + other.imaginary)
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{value}\;\;\KWD{object} \TYP{Complex}(\KWD{settable} \VAR{real}\COLONOP\TYP{Double}, \KWD{settable} \VAR{imaginary}\COLONOP\TYP{Double}=0)\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{opr} +(\KWD{self},\VAR{other}\COLONOP\TYP{Complex}) = \TYP{Complex}(\VAR{real} + \VAR{other}.\VAR{real}, \VAR{imaginary} + \VAR{other}.\VAR{imaginary})\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
When a mutable variable \VAR{z}:
%var z : Complex = Complex(0)
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{var} z \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \TYP{Complex} = \TYP{Complex}(0)\)
\end{Fortress}
updates its \VAR{imaginary} field, the following syntax:
%z.imaginary := v
\begin{Fortress}
\(z.\VAR{imaginary} \ASSIGN v\)
\end{Fortress}
can be used as an abbreviation for:
%z := Complex(z.real, v)
\begin{Fortress}
\(z \ASSIGN \TYP{Complex}(z.\VAR{real}, v)\)
\end{Fortress}
So the setter for the field \VAR{imaginary} in \TYP{Complex} would do the
work of constructing and returning
%Complex(z.real, v)
\EXP{\TYP{Complex}(z.\VAR{real}, v)}, and the assignment:
%z.imaginary := v
\begin{Fortress}
\(z.\VAR{imaginary} \ASSIGN v\)

IntLiteral is now a subtype of ZZ32 (and thus of every other numeric
type).  But there are a number of caveats:
* ZZ32 is now a trait, with subtypes Int and IntLiteral.  In practice

This means that when you stuff the results into a polymorphically-typed
container (such as Maybe or List) the type variable will invariably be
dynamically instantiated with Int, rather than ZZ32 as you'd expect.
Most of the changes in this checkin address this in the regression
tests.

<!-- A design review for the curator's decision, before the switch-over's work is planned, on which run-time class carries each built-in type of the interpreter's library on the compiled path (the rehearsal's walls W2, W12, W13 and W14), written 2026-11-13 by a Fable worker, reading only, with one compiled probe: nine ways from the language, the two libraries, the code generator and the run time, each shown on `ZZ32`, `Boolean`, `String` and `Float`, with what it changes, what it does for unboxed numbers, whether it can be undone, what the team's texts say by provenance, and what Scala, Kotlin, Swift and Julia do; the ways sorted, and a recommendation: the object's class carries the value and the trait stays an interface (walk's own way), with the merge of each number trait and its one object as a second step for the curator to rule on. -->

# Which class carries a built-in type on the compiled path: the ways

## The answer in short

- A carrier is the JVM class whose instances are the values of a built-in type at run time. Today `FZZ32`, a class written by hand in Java, carries the prelude's `ZZ32`.
- The two libraries declare a built-in type in two shapes. The prelude says `trait ZZ32`, and `FZZ32` is the trait's class. The interpreter's library says `trait ZZ32 comprises { Int }` with `value object Int extends ZZ32`, and `value object Boolean` with no trait at all.
- I found nine ways. Four give the type its class (A to D). Three are ruled out (E, F, G). Two are later layers for speed, not carriers (H, I).
- The four that count:
  - **A.** The trait's class is written by hand, and the objects leave the library. This is the prelude's way, whole.
  - **B.** The trait's class is written by hand, and an empty object stands below each trait. This is the rehearsal's hack.
  - **C.** The object's class carries the value. The trait stays a plain interface. The library's text does not change. This is walk's own way, brought to the compiled path.
  - **D.** One object per type: each number trait is merged with its one object, as `NN32`, `RR32`, `Boolean` and `Char` already are. Then C's machinery, with one name per type.
- The team's later word, the library as the team wrote it, and the peers do not point to one way. The library as written points to C. The peers point to D. The team's later code is A's shape, but its author called it a special case "for the time being", and its own plan for unboxing is written over objects and `comprises` clauses, which is C's and D's shape.
- I recommend C now, and D as a second step that the curator rules on apart. C changes no line of the library, keeps walk as it is, removes W13 and W14 by construction, and closes the hole of ledger row 866. It gives up the prelude's trick of one hand-written class per type with no change in the code generator: the code generator must learn that a native object has a payload.

## The words

- **Built-in type.** A type whose values the language's implementation makes, not a constructor call: the numbers, `Boolean`, `Char`, the flat string, and a few Java-backed values (a reader, a writer, an array's store).
- **Carrier.** The JVM class of a built-in type's values on the compiled path.
- **Payload.** The Java value inside a carrier: an `int` in `FZZ32`, a `double` in `FRR64`, a `java.lang.String` in `FJavaString`.
- **Box.** A carrier object on the heap. A number is unboxed where the compiled code holds the payload itself: a JVM `double` in a local, a field or an array.
- **Springboard.** The class `T$DefaultTraitMethods` that the code generator writes for a trait `T`. It holds the trait's method bodies. An object's class extends the springboard of the first trait that the object extends (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:885-906`).
- **Stub.** A Java source file that declares, empty, the classes that the code generator will write, so that hand-written Java can extend them before any Fortress is compiled: `ProjectFortress/src/fortress/CompilerBuiltin.java`.
- **Closed type.** A type that no program can extend: an object, or a trait whose `comprises` clause lists its only subtypes. An open type is a trait without such a clause.
- **Native component.** A component declared `native component`. The specification says that inside one "the syntax and semantics are implementation dependent" (`Specification/basic/components/source-code.tex:513-518`). The library's four are `FortressBuiltin`, `FlatString`, `Reflect` and `AnyType`.

## What stands today

### The prelude: a trait, and a class written by hand

    trait ZZ32 extends { Number, Equality[\ZZ32\], StandardTotalOrder[\ZZ32\] }
            excludes { ZZ64, RR32, RR64 }
        opr +(self, other:ZZ32): ZZ32 = jIntOverflowingAdd(self,other)
        ...
    end

(`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:662`.) Beside it, in Java:

    public final class FZZ32 extends fortress.CompilerBuiltin.ZZ32.DefaultTraitMethods
            implements fortress.CompilerBuiltin.ZZ32 {
        final int val;
        public int getValue() {return val;}
        public static FZZ32 make(int x) { return new FZZ32(x); }
        public RTTI getRTTI() { return RTTIc.ONLY; }
    }

(`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32.java:14-43`.)

- The code generator writes the interface `fortress/CompilerBuiltin$ZZ32` and its springboard from the trait.
- `FZZ32` extends that springboard. So the Java build needs the stub file.
- A table says that the type `ZZ32` is written `FZZ32` in every descriptor: `compiler/NamingCzar.java:582-598`, and a copy for the run in `runtimeSystem/Naming.java:294-306`.
- The class of `Box[\ZZ32\]` is named with the carrier: `Box⟦com|sun|fortress|compiler|runtimeValues|FZZ32⟧` (`runtimeSystem/Instantiater.java:56`).
- Fifteen names are carried so: `Boolean`, `Character`, `ZZ`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ32`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `RR32`, `RR64`, `JavaString`, `JavaBufferedReader`, `JavaBufferedWriter`, `ZZ32Vector`, `StringVector` and `()`.

The prelude's trait is open. A program may write `object MyNum extends ZZ32`. The checker takes it, the compile exits 0, and the run dies: 'IncompatibleClassChangeError: class OpenZ$MyInt can not implement com.sun.fortress.compiler.runtimeValues.FZZ32, because it is not an interface'. Ledger row 866 holds this. I ran it again today (section "The probe").

### The interpreter's library: five shapes

1. **A trait with one native object below it.** Five types.

       trait ZZ32 extends { AnyIntegral, Integral[\ZZ32\], Index }
               excludes { ZZ64, ZZ, NN64, NN32 }
               comprises { Int }
           asFloat(self): RR64
           opr =(self, b:ZZ32):Boolean = builtinPrimitive("...simpleIntArith.intEQ")
           ...
       end

   (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:775-777`.)

       value object Int extends ZZ32
           getter asString(): String = builtinPrimitive("...simpleIntArith.intToString")
           asFloat(self): RR64 = builtinPrimitive("...simpleIntArith.intToDouble")
       end

   (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:379-386`.) The five pairs: `ZZ32` and `Int`, `ZZ64` and `Long` (`:388`), `ZZ` and `BigNum` (`:544`), `NN64` and `UnsignedLong` (`:533`), `RR64` and `Float` (`:61`). The object holds little for four of them: `asString`, `asExprString`, `asFloat`. For `RR64` it holds everything: `Float` has 146 lines of arithmetic.
2. **A native object alone.** `value object Boolean` (`FortressBuiltin.fss:554`), `value object Char` (`:590`), `value object NN32` (`:427`), `value object RR32` (`:212`), and `object FlatString` (`Library/FlatString.fss:34`). No trait stands above.
3. **`String`.** A trait (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4511`) with four objects: the native `FlatString`, and the plain `CatString`, `EmptyString` and `SubString` (`Library/String.fss:75`, `:282`, `:353`).
4. **A trait with a plain object.** `trait QQ comprises { Ratio }` and `value object Ratio(num: ZZ, den: ZZ)` (`FortressLibrary.fss:554-557`, `:648`). `Ratio` is ordinary Fortress. It needs no carrier in any way.
5. **A Java-backed trait with a private native object.** `JavaBufferedWriter`, `JavaBufferedReader`, `JavaArrayStore`, `JavaRR64ArrayStore` (`FortressLibrary.fss:1987`, `:1998`, `:2442`, `:2448`), each with a private object in `FortressBuiltin` (`:55`, `:58`, `:720`, `:725`). The revival made these (P-164, P-169, F-330, F-333).

Under walk, a native object's values come from a Java class of the object's own name. `BuildNativeEnvironment.nativeConstructor` builds the class name from the component's line `private package="com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim"` and the object's name (`interpreter/evaluator/BuildNativeEnvironment.java:42-57`; `FortressBuiltin.fss:15-16`). So walk's rule is: **in a native component, a class written by hand is the object's class.** `glue/prim/Int.java` is `Int`'s, and its values are `FInt` objects.

Walk already treats `Int` and `ZZ32` as one type where it matters. It reads a value of `Int` at `ZZ32` where it infers a static argument, so `Cell(3)` is a `Cell[\ZZ32\]`, and it prints `ZZ32` (F-344, F-328).

## What the rehearsal met

The rehearsal of 2026-11-10 switched a scratch tree's compiled path onto the interpreter's library (`explorations/compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/switch-rehearsal.md`). Four of its walls are this design.

- **W2.** The wrappers of the helper classes cannot name a class for `FortressLibrary$String` or `FortressLibrary$ZZ32`. Behind that: thirteen hand-written classes extend the prelude's springboards by name; five carried types are objects, and a hand-written class cannot extend an object; the stores have no Fortress value; `FlatString`'s classes cannot be stubbed in Java.
- **W12.** A carried type has two names at run time. The trait's `RTTIc` holds the trait's interface. The descriptors hold the carrier. A static argument read from a value named the first; the classes were made under the second.
- **W13.** `asFloat` has no body on a compiled `ZZ32`: the trait declares it, the object `Int` defines it, and the carrier was the trait's class.
- **W14.** `Float extends RR64` became an interface that extends the class `FRR64`: the code generator names a carried type by its carrier in an `extends` clause too.

The rehearsal's hack for W2 turned the five objects into traits with `comprises { XCarrier }` and an empty object. That broke walk in the scratch tree. Its hack for W13 copied `asFloat` into `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`, and made `Float` a trait.

All four walls come from one mismatch: the prelude's way puts the class on the trait, and the interpreter's library puts the values on the object.

## The ways

Each way is shown on `ZZ32` first, then on `Boolean` (an object alone), `String`, and `Float` (a number below a number trait). The costs are by reading, not built. A rung is one unit of the record's work, with its tests.

### Way A. The trait's class is written by hand, and the objects leave the library

This is the prelude's way, carried over whole.

**On `ZZ32`.** The library's text changes:

    trait ZZ32 extends { AnyIntegral, Integral[\ZZ32\], Index }
            excludes { ZZ64, ZZ, NN64, NN32, ... }
        asFloat(self): RR64 = builtinPrimitive("...simpleIntArith.intToDouble")
        getter asString(): String = builtinPrimitive("...simpleIntArith.intToString")
        ...
    end

`Int` is deleted, and its three bodies move into the trait. In Java:

    public final class FZZ32 extends fortress.FortressLibrary.ZZ32.DefaultTraitMethods
            implements fortress.FortressLibrary.ZZ32 { final int val; ... }

**On `Boolean`.** `value object Boolean` becomes `trait Boolean`, with `FBoolean` as today. The same for `Char`, `NN32`, `RR32` and `FlatString`.

**On `String`.** `String` stays a trait with its three plain objects. `FlatString` becomes a trait that `FJavaString` carries. This is the prelude's `trait JavaString extends String`.

**On `Float`.** `Float`'s 146 lines move into `trait RR64`, over the bodies that `RR64` has today. `FRR64` carries `RR64`.

**The rule that blocks it.** A trait is open. An object excludes every type that it does not extend; a trait excludes only what its `excludes` clause lists. When the rehearsal made the five objects traits, the apis failed the overloading check with 15 errors, such as 'Invalid overloading of || in trait FlatString: (FlatString, Char)->String and (String, Number)->String' (its W2). The prelude gets around this by writing an `excludes` list on every built-in trait by hand: `trait NN64 ... excludes { ZZ32, ZZ64, RR32, RR64, NN32, ZZ }` (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:818`). Steele called this "quadratic blow-up" in 2016 (`research/extracts/SteeleJuliaCon2016-extract.md:356-365`). And the lists do not close the type: row 866.

**What it changes.**

- The library's text: five objects deleted, five objects made traits, about 250 lines moved, an `excludes` list on each of ten traits. The `comprises` clauses of the five number traits go.
- Walk: its values need an object type. `FInt` is made by `Int`'s constructor class. With no object, walk's native constructors, its carriers of `self` (`interpreter/glue/StaticNativeApp.java`) and the reading of F-344 are rebuilt for traits. This is the largest part.
- The code generator: nothing new for the carriers. The tables are renamed.
- The run-time classes: thirteen classes re-parented, three stub files, as the rehearsal did.
- The loader: no change.
- The tests: `tests/LanguageTypeInstancesWalk` and each test that names `Int`, `Float` or the others as a type. The checker's count and the distance must reach 0 again after the `excludes` lists.

**Speed later.** It hinders. An unboxed `RR64` needs the compiler to know that a value of static type `RR64` is exactly one class. An open trait does not say so, so the code generator would have to treat the fifteen names as special for ever, against the checker's own view. Dispatch on a built-in type tests one final class, as today.

**Undo.** Costly. The library's and walk's text are rewritten. Going back means writing the objects again.

**The team's texts.** For: the prelude's source and the run time are this way, built alike for all its types from 2009 to 2012. Against: its author called it a special case for the time being; the reasons that made the prelude's types traits are gone; the specification calls a primitive a value object. The section "What the team's texts say" gives each with its date.

### Way B. The trait's class is written by hand, and an empty object stands below each trait

This is the rehearsal's hack, made a design.

**On `ZZ32`.**

    trait ZZ32 ... comprises { Int }
        asFloat(self): RR64 = builtinPrimitive("...intToDouble")   (* moved up from Int *)
        ...
    end
    value object Int extends ZZ32 end                              (* empty *)

`FZZ32` extends `ZZ32`'s springboard, as in way A. The empty object keeps the trait closed for the checker.

**On `Boolean`.** `trait Boolean comprises { BooleanCarrier }` with `object BooleanCarrier extends Boolean end`, and `FBoolean` on the trait.

**On `String`.** `trait FlatString extends String comprises { FlatStringCarrier }`, and `FJavaString` on the trait.

**On `Float`.** `trait RR64 comprises { Float }` takes `Float`'s 146 lines; `Float` is left empty.

**What blocks it.** The object is a declaration with no values on the compiled path, and with all the values under walk. The rehearsal says that its hack "breaks walk in the scratch tree, which binds these objects' natives". W12 stays: the type still has two names.

**What it changes.** The library's text as in way A, plus five new empty objects. Walk: its natives move from the objects to the traits, or the two paths read two texts, which P-37 forbids. The code generator, the run-time classes and the loader as in way A.

**Speed later.** The trait is closed, so it leaves unboxing open. But the code generator must still know that the trait's class is `FZZ32` and not the listed object's.

**Undo.** As way A.

**The team's texts.** None shows a trait with an empty comprised object. It is in no text.

### Way C. The object's class carries the value, and the trait stays an interface

This is walk's way, brought to the compiled path. The library's text does not change.

**On `ZZ32`.** The declarations stay as they are today. The code generator compiles them as it compiles any trait and object, with one addition for a native object:

    interface fortress/FortressLibrary$ZZ32                      (from trait ZZ32)
    final class fortress/FortressBuiltin$Int implements ...$ZZ32 (from value object Int)
        final int val;
        static Int make(int)        int getValue()

- The carrier is `Int`'s class. It has `asFloat`'s body, because `Int` declares it. So W13 does not arise.
- `Int extends ZZ32` names the interface, as every `extends` clause does. Nothing extends a carrier, because nothing extends an object. So W14 does not arise.
- A table gives each native object its payload: `Int` an `int`, `Float` a `double`, `FlatString` a `java.lang.String`, `BigNum` a `BigInteger`. This is the table of `NamingCzar` today, keyed by the object.
- One rule answers W12: a value of a native object is read at its trait where a static argument is formed, and the stamped class is named by the carrier. Walk has this rule (F-344). The checker already lets a value of `trait T comprises { O }` stand where `O` is expected (the rehearsal's W7).
- A value of static type `ZZ32` is exactly an `Int`, because the trait says `comprises { Int }`. So a descriptor for `ZZ32` may name `Int`'s class, as a descriptor names `FZZ32` today. The cast that row 307 asks for is the same knowledge.

**On `Boolean`.** `value object Boolean` compiles to its own class, with a `boolean` payload. Its methods written in Fortress (`cond`, `generate`, `=`) are the object's methods. No trait, no second name.

**On `String`.** `String` is an interface. `FlatString`'s class holds a `java.lang.String`. `CatString`, `EmptyString` and `SubString` are plain classes. A helper's Java `String` result becomes a `FlatString` value. Walk refuses a helper parameter declared `String` other than `self` (the skill's `references/interpreter.md`, "Natives"), so the library's bindings take `FlatString`, and no wrapper needs to cast a `String` down.

**On `Float`.** `Float`'s class holds a `double` and has its 146 lines as its own methods. `RR64` is an interface. A call `x + y` on two `RR64` values dispatches to `Float`'s `+`, as under walk.

**Where the class comes from: three forms.** This choice is inside way C.

1. Written by hand, extending the object's generated springboard, as `FZZ32` extends the trait's today. It needs the stub files, and `FlatString` cannot be stubbed in Java (the rehearsal's W2: Java allows no class `FlatString` nested in a class `FlatString`).
2. Written by the code generator, over a small payload class written by hand: `abstract class FZZ32 extends FValue { final int val; getValue() }`, and the generated `Int extends FZZ32`. No stub is needed, because the hand-written class extends nothing generated. The run time's Java keeps a name to test, as `nativeHelpers/equalityRule.java:38` tests `instanceof FZZ32`. The object then takes its traits' default methods by forwarding methods, which the code generator already writes for every trait after the first (`CodeGen.java:885-906`).
3. Written whole by the code generator, with the payload as a hidden field. The run time's Java then reaches the payload through a small interface.

Form 2 looks best to me: no stubs, and the box's chain of constructors is three classes, `Int`, `FZZ32`, `FValue`. Today's chain through the one library's springboards is six, which leaves a margin of two frames before HotSpot stops removing temporary boxes (F-302). Not measured.

**What blocks it.** The code generator compiles an object without value parameters as a singleton, one instance. A native object has many values. The specification leaves a native component's meaning to the implementation, and walk uses that freedom in the same place. So the block is in the code generator only, and it gets around it as walk does: by the component's `native` mark and a table.

**What it changes.**

- The library's text: nothing. (`NN32`'s `zero` and `one`, the rehearsal's W4, are a defect apart.)
- Walk: nothing.
- The code generator: a native object gets a payload, `make` and `getValue`, and many instances; the tables are keyed by the object; a trait with one comprised native object is named by that object's class in descriptors; the wrapper generator's converters read the same table. About three rungs, the rehearsal's own estimate for W2's repair, with W12's rule among them.
- The run-time classes: the thirteen become payload classes (form 2) or are re-parented (form 1). `equalityRule`, `FValue.asString`, `Utility` and `FException` name the new classes. The helpers' 99 raise strings change in every way.
- The loader: the run's copy of the table (`Naming.java`), and one canonical name for a stamp.
- The tests: the compiled tests stay. New tests: `typecase x of Int`, `Box(3)` as a `Box[\ZZ32\]` compiled, a program's `object MyNum extends ZZ32` refused by the checker (row 866's test promoted).

**Speed later.** It helps.

- The type is closed in the language itself. So "a value of static type `RR64` is a `double`" is sound, and the code generator can choose unboxed arithmetic by static type (PLAN's phase 6, decision B; P-17).
- In a field: a field declared `RR64` in a plain object can become a `double` field. A field of type `T` in `Box[\T\]` needs the loader to stamp a different class (F-18); the canonical name of W12's rule is what it would key on.
- In an array: the store is already a `double[]` (`JavaRR64ArrayStore`, F-333; P-84). The carrier decides only which box `get` returns until phase 6.
- Across a call: a function `f(x: RR64): RR64` can take the descriptor `(D)D`, because no other class can arrive.
- Dispatch on a built-in type tests one final class, as today. With the closed type, the test can be dropped where the static type is the trait.
- The team's bytecode optimizer finds a box by the methods `make` and `getValue` on a carried type (`compiler/asmbytecodeoptimizer/MethodInsn.java:71-85`). Way C keeps both names.

**Undo.** Cheap. The library and walk are untouched. Going to way D later is additive. Going to way A later costs what way A costs today.

**The team's texts.** For: the interpreter's library as written; walk's native components; the specification's value objects and its `trait Boolean ... comprises { ... }`; Chase's unboxing plan of 2009, whose cases are objects and `comprises`. Against: the prelude and its run time put the class on the trait.

### Way D. One object per type: each number trait merged with its one object

This is the library's own way for `NN32`, `RR32`, `Boolean` and `Char`, applied to the five number traits. It is way C plus one change of the library's text.

**On `ZZ32`.**

    value object ZZ32 extends { AnyIntegral, Integral[\ZZ32\], Index }
        coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) = v.asZZ32
        asFloat(self): RR64 = builtinPrimitive("...simpleIntArith.intToDouble")
        opr =(self, b:ZZ32):Boolean = builtinPrimitive("...simpleIntArith.intEQ")
        ...
    end

`Int` is gone. The `excludes` and `comprises` clauses go too: an object excludes every type that it does not extend. The class:

    final class ZZ32 { final int val; ... }     (one declaration, one class, one name)

**On `Boolean`.** Nothing changes: it is already this shape. The same for `Char`, `NN32`, `RR32`.

**On `String`.** Nothing changes: `String` has four objects, so it stays a trait, as in way C.

**On `Float`.** `value object RR64` takes `Float`'s 146 lines. About 40 bodies of `trait RR64` go: `opr +(self,b:RR64):RR64 = asFloat(self) + asFloat(b)` and its like (`FortressLibrary.fss:431-450`). They served when `RR64` had four subtypes. Today every `RR64` is a `Float`, so `Float`'s own `+` is always the more specific one and these bodies never run.

**Why the split is there.** It was made for two reasons, and both are gone.

- Maessen split `ZZ32` on 2008-07-15 so that `IntLiteral` could be a subtype of `ZZ32` (`fca589bbb0`: "ZZ32 is now a trait, with subtypes Int and IntLiteral"). The numerals have their own types now (P-173, P-174), and `IntLiteral` left the library.
- The other traits had subtypes by nesting: `trait ZZ64 ... comprises { Long, ZZ32 }` at the team's last commit. The tower is flat now (P-43).

So each of the five traits has exactly one object, and the split serves nothing that the record names.

**What blocks it.** Under walk, an object with native values must be in a native component. `FortressLibrary` is not one. So the five move into `FortressBuiltin`, beside `NN32` and `RR32`, or walk learns one more place. The names `Int`, `Long`, `Float`, `BigNum` and `UnsignedLong` go: the library names them on 4, 4, 41, 4 and 4 lines, almost all in their own declarations, and I found no test or model line that uses one as a type.

**What it changes.**

- The library's text: five objects deleted, five traits made objects and moved, about 600 lines moved, about 40 dead bodies deleted.
- Walk: five constructor classes renamed; the reading of F-344 and the ilk names of F-328 become needless for the numbers and stay for the strings.
- The code generator: as way C, without the rule for a trait with one comprised object, and without W12's rule for the numbers.
- The run-time classes and the loader: as way C.
- The tests: `tests/LanguageTypeInstancesWalk` and `tests/FlatTowerRungF` change where they name the objects. The checker's count and the distance are run again. I did not run them: this is the first probe to make before the way is chosen.

**Speed later.** As way C, and a little more: one declaration per operator instead of two, so the dispatch method of `+` has one arm less for each number type, and the static type is the class with no rule in between.

**Undo.** The merge is mechanical each way, but it changes text that the team wrote. From C, it can be taken at any time. From D back to C, the objects are written again.

**The team's texts.** For: `NN32` (Steele, 2008), `RR32` (Ryu, 2008), `Boolean` and `Char` are this shape in the library; the prelude's first number types were objects (Flood, 2009-03-03); the library's own complaint about `Float` against `RR64` (below); every peer. Against: the specification's api style shows a built-in type as a trait with hidden comprised types; the split is the team's text, though its reasons are gone.

### Way E. The payload written in the library's text

    value object Int(v: JavaInt32) extends ZZ32
        asFloat(self): RR64 = intToDouble(self.v)
    end

The object is plain Fortress, and its one field has a Java-backed type. The code generator writes the class as for any object. The library does this for `Ratio(num: ZZ, den: ZZ)`, for the I/O objects over `JavaBufferedWriter` (P-164) and for the arrays over `JavaArrayStore` (F-333).

**What blocks it.** It does not end. `JavaInt32` is itself a built-in type that needs a carrier, by one of the other ways. The language has no type for a Java `int`: the specification lists a foreign-function interface among the things to do (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:706-710`; P-58), and the prelude's `import java` reads a Java `int` back as `ZZ32` itself (`NamingCzar.java:438-439`). So way E adds a second box around the first. That hinders speed until fields are unboxed.

It is the right way for a type made of other types, and the library already uses it there. It is not a way for the numbers.

### Way F. The JDK's own classes as carriers

`ZZ32` is `java.lang.Integer`, `String` is `java.lang.String`, as Kotlin does for a boxed `Int`.

**What blocks it.** Every Fortress value implements the interface `fortress/AnyType$Any` and answers `getRTTI()` (`compiler/runtimeValues/FValue.java:14-19`). A JDK class cannot implement an interface of ours. The team wraps instead: 'because we know these types are already loaded and not eligible for ASM-wrapping' (`NamingCzar.java:416-419`). To get around it, `Any` would be erased to `java.lang.Object` and the type of a value found from its class. The team's paper names that erasure only for union types (`Papers/Implementation/TypeMapping.tex:177`). It would change dispatch, RTTI and every descriptor. Ruled out by cost.

### Way G. The prelude's built-in types kept as a compiled-only component

The compiled path keeps a small `CompilerBuiltin` with the carried traits, and the one library's `ZZ32` is an alias of it.

**What blocks it.** P-37 deletes the prelude's three files. A `type` alias stops its component on both paths (row 18). And walk would read another text than the compiled path. Ruled out.

### Way H. No class: a JVM primitive, chosen by static type

A local of type `RR64` is a JVM `double`; `f(x: RR64): RR64` is `(D)D`; the box is made only where the value meets `Any`, a trait above it or a type parameter. Scala and Kotlin do this.

This is not a carrier. It is the layer that P-17 requires and that PLAN's phase 6 names as decision B. A box class is still needed, and ways A to D say which. The team planned this layer: Chase's `Unbox.java` (below), and the six names of `NamingCzar.java:262-280`, of which the third is "I, the signature encoding of Java int". It needs the type closed: ways C and D give that by the language, way B by its empty object, way A not at all.

### Way I. Classes specialised by the loader

`Box⟦RR64⟧` gets a `double` field, where today the loader only renames `T` to `FRR64` (F-18). The loader's stub for it is empty: '// Here will go all the magic expando-stuff.' (`runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172`). C# does this.

Also a later layer, not a carrier: way A4 of the array decision (P-85). It keys on the name of the static argument in a stamp, so it needs W12 answered, which every way must do.

### Is the prelude's carrier the team's later decision, type by type (P-37)

P-37 says that the one library takes a design of the prelude's where it is the team's later decision. P-26 says what counts: code "where the team built it alike for all its types" counts, and code "that its author called a stub", or that works around a limit, does not.

The prelude's carrier has two parts, and they answer differently.

- **The class: a final class that holds one JVM primitive, with `make` and `getValue`.** Later, built alike for all the types, and kept by every way here. Yes, it is the team's later decision, and ways A to D all take it.
- **The class put on a trait, with no object.** Later in date for every type. But I read it as not a decision of the language, for four reasons: its author called it a special case "for the time being" (2012); the number traits became traits to nest and to hold the literals, and both reasons are gone from both libraries; the open trait lets a program break the run (row 866); and the team's own unboxing plan has no case for it. P-26 has a clause on each side here, so the reading is the curator's to rule.

By type:

- `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `RR32`, `RR64`: an object first (`b2880c05c2`, 2009-03-03), a trait from `76c267f987` (2009-03-30), flat from `6896886fbc` (2009-08-31). The interpreter's `Int`, `Long`, `Float` and `RR32` are of 2008. Later in date; the trait form came from nesting and literals. Not a later decision, in my reading.
- `Boolean`: a trait in the prelude from 2009-04-15 at the latest (`bfa396091b`, Flood). The interpreter's object is of 2007. The same reading.
- `Character`: a trait from `7bc4e5e597` (2011-06-16). The interpreter's `Char` is of 2007. The carrier: the same reading. The name `Character` is Steele's later word, 'as in Fortress spec 1.0 beta' (`c2c769094c`); it is outside this review.
- `String` and `JavaString`: the two libraries agree. `String` is a trait, and a flat leaf holds a Java string: the prelude's `JavaString`, the library's `FlatString`, which Maessen renamed from `JavaString` on 2009-01-05 (`5335ab745d`). The leaf was an object in the prelude until 2011-11-17 (`2eb54ef20a`). Nothing to take but the trait form of the leaf: the same reading.
- `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`: traits by Tristan, 2011-11-23 and 2012-01-03, on the pattern. The interpreter's objects are of July 2008. The same reading.
- `JavaBufferedReader`, `JavaBufferedWriter`: Steele, 2011-07-12. Already taken: P-164 gave the one library the prelude's two traits by name and method. Under way C their carrier is the private object's class, not the trait's.

## The peers

Context only.

- **Scala.** `Int` is declared `final abstract class Int extends AnyVal`: one final type, no interface above it. The compiler maps it to a JVM `int` and boxes it to `java.lang.Integer` where it meets `Any` or a type parameter. A value class (`class Meter(val v: Double) extends AnyVal`) is a one-field wrapper that the compiler erases to its field.
- **Kotlin.** `Int` is a final class of the standard library with intrinsic members. It is a JVM `int` where it is not nullable and not a type argument, and a `java.lang.Integer` elsewhere. `@JvmInline value class` is the one-field wrapper.
- **Swift.** `struct Int { var _value: Builtin.Int64 }` in the standard library: a struct over a compiler's builtin type, with its operators written in the library over builtin operations, and protocols joined by extension. This is way E with a real bottom type, which Fortress lacks.
- **Julia.** `primitive type Int64 <: Signed 64 end`: a concrete, final leaf below abstract types (`Signed`, `Integer`, `Real`, `Number`). Only an abstract type can have subtypes. Arrays of such leaves are stored inline, and code is specialised for each concrete type.

All four make the built-in type itself one final, concrete type: way D's shape. Julia's abstract types above a final leaf are way C's and D's shape for `Number` and `AnyIntegral`. None has a second name for the same values. Scala and Kotlin show way H over it.

## The ways sorted

**Ruled out.**

- E, for the numbers: it does not end, since the payload's type needs a carrier too. It stays the library's way for `Ratio`, the I/O objects and the arrays.
- F: every value must implement `Any` and answer its RTTI, and a JDK class cannot.
- G: P-37 deletes the prelude, and row 18.
- B: it breaks walk or makes the two paths read two texts (P-37), and no text of the team shows it.

**Not carriers.** H and I are the layers of phase 6. They need a closed type and one canonical name. They are reasons among A to D, not alternatives to them.

**Standing: A, C, D.** Where the three grounds point:

- The team's later word. The prelude's code is A's shape. Its author's paper calls that shape a special case for the time being, and gives "an object is a final class" as the rule. The team's unboxing plan is C's and D's shape. So the later word splits: the later code says A, the later texts say C or D.
- The library as the team wrote it. C: it is the only way that changes none of its lines. Inside the library, `NN32`, `RR32`, `Boolean` and `Char` are D's shape, and the five split traits are C's.
- The peers. D.

They do not agree on one way. They agree on this much: the value's class belongs to a closed, final type. A is the only standing way that does not give that.

## Recommendation

Take way C now, in its form 2, and put way D to the curator as a second decision, after a probe. Way C compiles the library that the team wrote without changing a line of it, leaves walk alone, removes W13 and W14 by construction, answers W12 with the rule that walk already has (F-344), and closes row 866, because the checker reads the library's `comprises { Int }`. It gives the last phase what it needs for an unboxed `RR64` in a field, in an array and across a call: a type that the language itself closes. It can be undone at the cost of the code generator's table. What it gives up: the prelude's economy, where a hand-written class extends a trait's springboard and the code generator knows nothing; under C the code generator must learn that a native object has a payload and many values, about three rungs by reading, and the thirteen run-time classes change in any case. It also keeps two names for five number types, `ZZ32` and `Int`, with one rule on each path to hold them together. Way D removes that rule and about 40 dead bodies, and matches every peer, but it rewrites text of the team's whose reasons are gone and not whose authorship is; it should wait for one probe, the checker's count and walk's suites on a library with `ZZ32` and `RR64` merged, and for the curator's reading of P-26 on the split.
